{{short description|Japanese mathematician}}
{{more footnotes|date=August 2013}}

{{nihongo|'''Goro Nishida'''|西田 吾郎|Nishida Gorō|18 September 1943, in [[Osaka]] – 2 June 2014}} was a Japanese mathematician. He was a leading member of the [[Japan]]ese school of [[homotopy theory]], following in the tradition of [[Hiroshi Toda]].<ref name="jiji">{{Cite news|url=http://www.jiji.com/jc/c?g=obt_30&k=2014060300732 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20140603125316/http://www.jiji.com/jc/c?g=obt_30&k=2014060300732 |url-status=dead |archive-date=2014-06-03 |title=西田吾郎氏死去（京都大名誉教授・代数トポロジー、京都大元副学長） |publisher=[[Jiji Press]] |date=2014-06-03 |accessdate=2014-06-03 }}</ref>

Nishida received his [[Ph.D.]] from [[Kyoto University]] in 1973, after spending the 1971–72 academic year at the [[University of Manchester]] in [[England]]. He then became a professor at Kyoto University in 1990.<ref>[https://nrid.nii.ac.jp/nrid/1000000027377/ NISHIDA Goro / KAKEN] {{in lang|ja}}</ref> His proof in 1973 of Michael Barratt's conjecture (that positive-degree elements in the [[Stable homotopy theory|stable homotopy]] ring of spheres are [[Nilpotence theorem|nilpotent]]) was a major breakthrough: following [[Frank Adams]]' [[Adams-Novikov spectral sequence|solution]] of the [[Hopf invariant]] one problem, it marked the beginning of a new global understanding of algebraic topology.

His contributions to the field were celebrated in 2003 at the NishidaFest<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://msp.warwick.ac.uk/gtm/2007/10/index.xhtml |title=Geometry & Topology Monograph, Volume 10 (2007) |access-date=2013-01-09 |archive-date=2014-06-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140617165903/http://www.msp.warwick.ac.uk/gtm/2007/10/index.xhtml |url-status=dead }}</ref> in [[Kinosaki, Hyōgo|Kinosaki]], followed by a satellite conference at the [[Nagoya Institute of Technology]]; the proceedings were published in ''[[Geometry and Topology]]''<nowiki>'</nowiki>s monograph series. In 2000 he was the leading organizer for a concentration year at the Japan–US Mathematics Institute<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mathematics.jhu.edu/JAMI9900/ |title=Home Page |accessdate=2013-08-06 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100605030307/http://www.mathematics.jhu.edu/JAMI9900/ |archivedate=2010-06-05 }}</ref> at [[Johns Hopkins University]].

Nishida's earliest work grew out of the study of infinite [[loop space]]s; his first paper (in 1968, on what came eventually to be known as the Nishida relations) accounts for interactions between [[Steenrod algebra|Steenrod operations]] and Kudo–Araki (Dyer–Lashof) operations. Some of his later work concerns a circle of ideas surrounding the [[Segal conjecture]], transfer homomorphisms, and stable splittings of [[classifying space]]s of groups. The ideas in this series of papers have by now grown into a rich subfield of homotopy theory; it continues today in (for example) the theory of [[p-compact group|''p''-compact group]]s.
